samples.text:
In recent years, the number of people who are overweight has increased in many countries. Some people think the government should put a tax on unhealthy food like sugary drinks and fast food, as they do with cigarettes. I agree with this idea to some extent.

On the one hand, a tax can make people buy less unhealthy food. When the price of something goes up, people usually buy less of it. For example, many people stopped smoking or smoked less when cigarettes became very expensive. The same thing can happen with fizzy drinks and burgers. Also, the government can use the money from this tax for hospitals and for health education in schools, which will help the whole society.

On the other hand, unhealthy food is not exactly the same like tobacco. Cigarettes are always harmful, but eating a pizza or a chocolate sometimes is not dangerous. The problem is only when people eat too much of it. So it is not fair to punish everybody who enjoy fast food occasionally. Moreover, this tax can be a problem for poor families, because cheap fast food is sometimes the only thing they can afford after a long working day, and fresh food is often more expensive.

In my opinion, the government should tax the most unhealthy products, such as sugary drinks, but not all fast food. At the same time, they should make healthy food more cheaper and teach people about good diet.

In conclusion, I partly agree that unhealthy food should be taxed like tobacco. A tax can reduce consumption and give money to health services, but it must be used together with other actions so that poor people are not affected too much.

samples.text:
Rising rates of obesity and diet-related illness have led some people to argue that governments should tax sugary drinks and fast food in the same way as tobacco. While I believe that taxes on certain unhealthy products can be useful, I disagree that such food should be treated exactly like tobacco.

There are clear arguments in favour of taxing unhealthy food. Price has a strong influence on consumer behaviour, and higher prices usually lead to reduced consumption, as has happened with cigarettes in many countries. A tax on sugary drinks, in particular, could discourage people from consuming large amounts of sugar without any real nutritional benefit. The revenue could also be used to fund public health campaigns or subsidise fruit and vegetables, which would make healthier choices more accessible.

However, food is fundamentally different from tobacco. There is no safe level of smoking, but most foods that are considered unhealthy are only harmful when eaten regularly and in large quantities. Taxing them heavily would therefore penalise the many people who consume them occasionally and responsibly. In addition, defining what counts as "unhealthy" is much more complicated than identifying a tobacco product; a burger made at a restaurant and one prepared at home may be quite similar, yet only one could realistically be taxed.

Such taxes may also have a disproportionate affect on low-income households, who spend a larger share of their income on food and often rely on cheap, processed meals. Unless the money raised is used to make healthy food more affordable, the policy could increase inequality without improving diets.

In conclusion, I support moderate, targeted taxes on products such as sugary drinks, but I do not agree that unhealthy food in general should be taxed as heavily as tobacco. Education and support for healthier choices are equally important.

samples.text:
With obesity and related conditions placing growing strain on health systems, some argue that governments should tax sugary drinks and fast food as they tax tobacco. I agree that fiscal measures have a role to play, particularly for sugar-sweetened beverages, but I believe equating unhealthy food with tobacco is both conceptually flawed and potentially counterproductive.

The case for taxation rests on sound principles. Consumers respond to price, and the dramatic decline in smoking in many countries owes much to sustained increases in tobacco duty. Sugary drinks are an especially suitable target: they provide calories with virtually no nutritional value, they are easy to define, and there is evidence that levies on them encourage manufacturers to reduce sugar content. Revenue raised in this way can be reinvested in school meals, sports facilities or subsidies for fresh produce, amplifying the health benefit.

Nevertheless, food differs from tobacco in crucial respects. Cigarettes are harmful in any quantity, whereas burgers, chips or chocolate are problematic only as part of an unbalanced diet. A tax modelled on tobacco would therefore treat moderate consumption as though it were inherently dangerous, which many people would reasonably regard as excessive state intervention. Moreover, "fast food" is a notoriously vague category, and drawing a line between a takeaway meal and a restaurant dish would invite both confusion and avoidance.

There is also the issue of fairness. Food taxes are regressive, weighing most heavily on households with the least disposable income, and in areas where fresh food is expensive or hard to obtain, higher prices may simply reduce families' budgets rather than change what they eat. Any such tax must therefore be paired with measures that make healthy alternatives genuinely affordable.

In conclusion, targeted taxes on clearly defined products like sugary drinks are justified, but applying a tobacco-style regime to unhealthy food in general would be neither fair nor effective.
